analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in two steps to $6.65 an hour.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the minimum wage in two steps to $6.65 an hour drew 104 House cosponsors but never received a vote, dying in committee before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from its then-current level in two steps: to $5.90 an hour shortly after passage, then to $6.65 an hour a year later. It would also have extended the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, gradually raising wages there until they matched the mainland standard. The bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the 108th Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, many of them in restaurants, retail, and other service jobs, would see their hourly pay rise in two steps to $6.65. The Northern Mariana Islands provision would gradually raise wages there from $3.55 an hour until they reached the federal level, ending the territory's exemption from the federal wage floor.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage to $5.90 an hour starting 60 days after enactment, and to $6.65 an hour one year after that.

It would apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, with a transition starting at $3.55 an hour and rising 50 cents every six months until it equals the federal minimum wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers, especially in restaurants, retail, and small businesses with thin margins, would face higher labor costs, some of which are typically passed on to customers through higher prices. Employers in the Northern Mariana Islands would face a staged increase as well.

drawbacks.text: Raising the wage floor raises labor costs for employers, particularly small businesses and restaurants that rely on low-wage entry-level work; economists debate how much of that cost shows up as reduced hiring for inexperienced workers or as higher prices for customers.

The bill raised the wage in two relatively quick steps with no tax offsets or small-business accommodations attached, which critics argued added to the cost shock for small employers; the bill text contains no offsetting relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers affected, the bill's benefit is direct and unambiguous: a pay raise of $1.50 an hour at full implementation. The main cost falls on employers who pay minimum wage, and the classic tradeoff is whether some entry-level jobs shrink or prices rise as a result. The bill included a transition period for the Northern Mariana Islands but no other phase-in relief or offsets for small business, which is the strongest good-faith objection to its design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2005 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2003 in the House on February 27, 2003.
The bill gathered 104 cosponsors — 103 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republicans.
On the day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On March 24, 2003, it was referred to the subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 108th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage kept paying the then-current lower rate for the rest of the Congress, and the committee leadership never had to allow a vote on the increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; no floor vote ever came

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA), bill sponsor and senior Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2003 and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 104 House cosponsors (103 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors within weeks of introduction; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and referred it to the Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it remained without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair, never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote during the 108th Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed legislation to raise the federal minimum wage during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 104 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; there were no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: These employers would have had to pay $6.65 an hour instead of the then-current rate, a direct cost increase. Ordinary minimum-wage workers would have gained exactly what these employers would have had to pay.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and service industries
industries.note: The bill would end the islands' exemption from the federal minimum wage, raising local wages from $3.55 an hour in staged 50-cent steps. The territory's exemption had historically let local employers, including garment manufacturers, pay well below the mainland wage floor.
